questions.stem: An engineer's design brief edits 'The server will be down from 2pm to 4pm for maintenance, please plan accordingly' to 'Server down 2-4pm for maintenance'; what is preserved?

options.text: The politeness of the original wording
The exact character count of the original
The essential facts: time and reason
The author's signature style

questions.explanation: The edit keeps time and reason; politeness, count, and style are secondary. Essential facts survive.
questions.hint: Check which facts remain after trimming.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise affiliate links as paid content
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief includes affiliate links in a review; does this need disclosure?

answer.exemplar: Yes, affiliate links earn commission on purchases, so they count as paid content and must be disclosed clearly before readers click or buy.

questions.explanation: Affiliate links earn commission, so they are paid content and need disclosure. Readers must know before clicking.
questions.hint: Treat commission-earning links as paid.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Spot review bombing patterns

stimulus.body: An engineer's design brief sees a product's rating drop from 4.5 to 2.1 in two days after a controversy unrelated to product quality. Most new reviews mention the controversy, not the product.

questions.stem: What is likely happening?

options.text: The product quality suddenly collapsed
Genuine users all had the same bad experience
A platform algorithm error
Review bombing driven by the controversy

questions.explanation: A sudden drop tied to an unrelated controversy suggests review bombing, not quality collapse. Genuine shared failure is unlikely.
questions.hint: Check whether reviews address the product or the controversy.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a report with only official sources
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief reads a report citing only government officials on a policy's success; what is weak?

options.text: Officials may overstate success
The report is too short
The policy is too new to judge
Readers dislike government sources

questions.explanation: Officials may overstate success, so their word alone is weak. Length, timing, and taste are not the sourcing issue.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sources have a stake in the outcome.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a fact-check's limits on predictions
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief sees a fact-check on a claim that 'the market will crash next month'; what can it verify?

options.text: Whether the prediction is guaranteed
options.misconception: assumes predictions can be verified now

options.text: Whether the author is trustworthy
Whether the cited data and reasoning are sound
Whether readers believe the claim

questions.explanation: A fact-check can test the data and reasoning behind a prediction, not the future outcome. Author and belief are not evidence.
questions.hint: Verify the basis, not the future.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a headline that frames by omission
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief rewrites 'No Injuries Reported' to 'Building Collapse Averted' for the same event; what changed?

answer.exemplar: The rewrite foregrounds the avoided disaster and downplays the absence of injuries, shifting attention from outcome to near-miss and raising alarm.

questions.explanation: The rewrite shifts focus from no injuries to a near-disaster, raising alarm. Foregrounding changes reader perception.
questions.hint: Compare which idea leads in each version.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Identify an ad using fear appeals

stimulus.body: An engineer's design brief watches an ad showing a home break-in and a family in distress, then offers a security system. The tone is urgent and the imagery is dark.

questions.stem: What emotion is the ad primarily leveraging?

options.text: Joy and celebration of safety
Trust in a famous spokesperson
Curiosity about technology
Fear of home intrusion

questions.explanation: The ad leverages fear of intrusion to sell security. Joy, curiosity, and spokesperson are not the drivers.
questions.hint: Identify the emotion before the product appears.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise when a thread is better than one post
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief has five distinct updates about one outage; how should they post?

options.text: A thread with one update per post
One post cramming all five updates
Five separate accounts posting
No posts until the outage ends

questions.explanation: A thread keeps updates readable and linked. Cramming, fragmenting, or withholding are worse.
questions.hint: Balance brevity with readability and timeliness.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise platform labels as disclosure
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief sees a post tagged 'Paid partnership with Brand'; what does this tag do?

options.text: It hides the post from followers
It guarantees the product is good
It discloses the paid relationship
It removes the need for further context

questions.explanation: The tag discloses the paid relationship. It does not hide, endorse quality, or remove context needs.
questions.hint: Read the label as transparency, not promotion.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Check review dates against product changes
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief reads 2021 reviews for a product revised in 2024; what caution applies?

answer.exemplar: Older reviews may describe the pre-2024 version, so they may not reflect current quality; check dates and look for recent reviews after the revision.

questions.explanation: Older reviews may describe an earlier version. Check dates and seek recent reviews.
questions.hint: Match review dates to product versions.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise when data beats anecdote

stimulus.body: An engineer's design brief reads a report about a new policy's effects. It quotes three unhappy residents and includes no statistics, surveys, or studies. The policy affects a city of two million.

questions.stem: What sourcing weakness is present?

options.text: The policy is too recent to cover
The residents are unhappy
The report is too long
The report lacks data beyond a few anecdotes

questions.explanation: Three anecdotes cannot represent two million people; data is missing. Sentiment, length, and timing are not the sourcing issue.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sample matches the population.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise when a fact-check rates a quote
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief sees a fact-check on a quote attributed to a politician; what is being verified?

options.text: Whether the politician's policy is good
Whether the politician is popular
Whether the politician actually said it

questions.explanation: The fact-check verifies whether the quote was actually said, not policy merit, popularity, or taste.
questions.hint: Verify attribution, not merit.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Identify a headline that frames by numbers
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief sees '90% of Users Satisfied' for a survey of 20 people; what is foregrounded?

options.text: The small sample behind the big percentage
The number of dissatisfied users
The survey's methodology
options.misconception: looks for method detail not present

options.text: The impressive percentage, hiding the small sample

questions.explanation: The headline foregrounds the impressive percentage and hides the tiny sample. Methodology is not shown.
questions.hint: Ask what the big number hides.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise an ad targeting caregivers
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief sees an ad for incontinence products showing adult children helping parents; who is targeted?

answer.exemplar: The ad targets adult children caring for ageing parents, using imagery and messaging that address caregiver concerns rather than the older adult alone.

questions.explanation: The imagery targets adult children caregivers, not the older adult alone. The buyer is the caregiver.
questions.hint: Identify who is being asked to buy.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the value of a clear call to action

stimulus.body: An engineer's design brief drafts a short post about a new feature. It explains the feature in one line but gives no next step. Readers ask 'how do I try it?' in replies.

questions.stem: What is missing from the post?

options.text: A clear call to action telling readers what to do next
A longer explanation of the feature
A list of every possible use case
The author's credentials

questions.explanation: A clear call to action tells readers what to do next. Longer explanations or credentials do not fix the missing step.
questions.hint: Add the next step, not more detail.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise that disclosure does not remove bias
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief sees a clearly labelled sponsored post; does disclosure make it unbiased?

options.text: Yes, because the label removes all influence
Yes, because readers now trust it fully
No, the post may still favour the sponsor
No, because all sponsored posts are lies

questions.explanation: Disclosure informs readers but does not remove possible bias. It is not a guarantee of truth or a lie.
questions.hint: Disclosure enables judgement; it does not ensure neutrality.
